check.why: With gefallen the shoes are the subject and the person who likes them is dative: mir.

tips.title: mir/dir for how you are, mich/dich for what is seen
tips.text: es geht mir, hilf mir, danke dir → dative. sieh mich, liebe dich → accusative. This first dative is small: learn its verbs and it can't go wrong.

examples.de: Ich liebe dich und ich helfe dir.
examples.en: I love you (acc.) and I help you (dat.).

examples.de: Siehst du mich? – Ja, und ich helfe dir gleich.
examples.en: Can you see me? – Yes, and I'll help you in a moment.

check.q: Informal, 'I'll see you tomorrow': Ich sehe ____ morgen.
check.why: sehen is not one of the dative verbs, so it takes the accusative dich.

remember: helfen, danken, gehören, gefallen, es geht — five triggers, all take mir/dir/Ihnen.
ihr = to her, ihnen = to them, Ihnen = to you — the h and the capital are the clues.

context.de: Guten Morgen, Frau Klein, wie geht es Ihnen? – Danke, gut. Und dir? – Mir geht es auch gut. Können Sie mir kurz helfen? Diese Tasche gehört mir nicht. – Sie gehört ihm, dem neuen Kollegen. – Ah, danke Ihnen!
context.en: Good morning, Mrs Klein, how are you? – Fine, thanks. And you? – I'm fine too. Can you help me a moment? This bag isn't mine. – It belongs to him, the new colleague. – Ah, thank you!

mistakes.why: es geht takes the dative pronoun.
helfen takes the dative.
danken takes the dative: Ihnen.

help.hook: One rule builds every German statement (the verb comes second), and five small words join your sentences together.
help.intro: One rule shapes every German statement: the conjugated verb is the second element. Not the second word — the second element. Ich fahre morgen nach Berlin, but start with tomorrow and the verb still comes second, so the subject moves behind it: Morgen fahre ich nach Berlin. English keeps subject-verb whatever comes first ('Tomorrow I go'); German swaps. The other half of basic sentence-building is joining sentences with the five little connectors that do not disturb that order: und (and), oder (or), aber (but), denn (because), dann (then). After und/oder/aber/denn the next sentence keeps its normal shape; dann counts as position 1, so the verb follows it: … dann gehe ich.

tips.title: Verb second — element, not word
tips.text: Whatever fills position 1 — subject, time, place — the verb is next and the subject, if it was displaced, comes straight after the verb.

examples.de: Ich fahre morgen nach Berlin. → Morgen fahre ich nach Berlin.
examples.en: I'm going to Berlin tomorrow. → Tomorrow I'm going to Berlin.

examples.de: Am Abend sehen wir fern.
examples.en: In the evening we watch TV.

tips.trap: 'Morgen ich fahre' is the signature English-speaker error. Front anything and the verb jumps ahead of the subject.

check.q: Heute Abend ____ ins Kino.
check.why: Heute Abend fills position 1, so the verb comes next and the subject moves behind it.

tips.title: und, oder, aber, denn — position 0
tips.text: These four join sentences without changing anything: Ich komme nicht, denn ich bin krank. The verb after them stays in its normal second place.

examples.de: Die Wohnung ist schön, aber sie ist teuer.
examples.en: The flat is nice, but it is expensive.

examples.de: Ich bleibe zu Hause, denn es regnet.
examples.en: I'm staying at home, because it's raining.

check.q: Ich lerne Deutsch, denn ____ in Berlin.
check.why: denn sits outside the sentence (position 0), so what follows keeps its normal order: subject, then verb.

tips.title: dann takes position 1
tips.text: dann is an adverb, so it fills the first slot and the verb follows: Zuerst esse ich, dann gehe ich. Same for deshalb, later.

examples.de: Ich dusche, dann frühstücke ich.
examples.en: I shower, then I have breakfast.

examples.de: Zuerst esse ich, dann gehe ich.
examples.en: First I eat, then I go.

check.q: Ich koche, dann ____.
check.why: dann takes position 1 itself, so the verb follows it straight away: dann esse ich.

tips.title: denn vs weil
tips.text: Both mean because. denn keeps normal order (denn ich bin krank); weil — coming later in the course — sends the verb to the end (weil ich krank bin). For now, use denn.

examples.de: Ich komme nicht, denn ich habe keine Zeit.
examples.en: I'm not coming, because I have no time.

examples.de: Ich bleibe zu Hause, denn es regnet.
examples.en: I'm staying at home, because it's raining.

check.q: Ich gehe zum Arzt, denn ____.
check.why: denn keeps normal order with the verb in second place. Verb-at-the-end order belongs to weil.

remember: Position 2 is the verb's seat. Whoever sits in seat 1, the verb is in seat 2.
und–oder–aber–denn don't count; dann does.

context.de: Am Morgen trinke ich Kaffee und esse ein Brötchen. Dann fahre ich zur Arbeit. Heute arbeite ich nur bis zwölf, denn ich habe einen Termin beim Arzt. Am Abend gehe ich ins Kino oder ich bleibe zu Hause – ich bin müde, aber der Film ist gut.
context.en: In the morning I drink coffee and eat a roll. Then I go to work. Today I'm only working until twelve, because I have a doctor's appointment. In the evening I'm going to the cinema or I'm staying at home – I'm tired, but the film is good.

mistakes.why: The verb must be the second element.
dann occupies position 1; the verb follows it.
denn does not change word order.

help.hook: With Ich hätte gern and a few shop phrases, you can buy bread, fruit or coffee anywhere German is spoken.
help.intro: Shopping out loud at the bakery, from the greeting to the goodbye: twelve lines of one conversation, short phrase to long. The single most useful sentence in it is Ich hätte gern … — 'I'd like …' — which works in every bakery, market stall, café and shop and you need it from day one even though the grammar behind it (Konjunktiv II) comes much later: you learn it as a fixed phrase, like a password. Alongside it: Was kostet das Brot? (how much is the bread?), Sonst noch etwas? (anything else?), Das ist alles, danke. Two sounds to practise: ö in Brötchen and schönen (round your lips, say 'eh'), and the open ä in hätte.

tips.title: Ich hätte gern … — the universal opener
tips.text: Followed by the thing in the accusative: Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee / ein Brötchen / zwei Kilo Äpfel. Softer than 'Ich will' and just as polite as 'Ich möchte' — shop staff hear both all day.

examples.de: Ich hätte gern ein Kilo Äpfel, bitte.
examples.en: I'd like a kilo of apples, please.

examples.de: Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee und ein Croissant.
examples.en: I'd like a coffee and a croissant.

check.q: Ich hätte gern ____ Kuchen. (der Kuchen)
check.why: The thing you ask for after Ich hätte gern is in the accusative, so masculine ein becomes einen.

tips.title: The shopkeeper's questions
tips.text: Was darf es sein? / Was möchten Sie? (what would you like?) — Sonst noch etwas? (anything else?) — Das macht … (that comes to …). Learn the answers: Das ist alles, danke. / Nein, danke.

examples.de: Sonst noch etwas? – Nein, danke, das ist alles.
examples.en: Anything else? – No thanks, that's all.

examples.de: Guten Tag! Was darf es sein?
examples.en: Hello! What can I get you?

check.q: The baker asks „Sonst noch etwas?“ You don't want anything else. What do you say?
check.why: Sonst noch etwas? means 'anything else?'. Das ist alles closes the order; Das macht … is what the baker says.

tips.title: ö and ä
tips.text: Brötchen, schönen: lips round, tongue for 'eh'. hätte: an open 'eh' as in 'bet'. Say 'Ich hätte gern zwei Brötchen' five times.

examples.de: Ich hätte gern zwei Brötchen.
examples.en: I'd like two rolls.

examples.de: Einen schönen Tag noch!
examples.en: Have a nice day!

check.q: Which word has the same rounded ö sound as Brötchen?
check.why: schön has the same ö: lips rounded as for 'o', tongue as for 'eh'. Sohn and Kuchen have plain o and u.

remember: 'Ich hätte gern' + accusative + 'bitte': a complete polite order, every time.
Was kostet das? — ask before you buy; the number comes back euros first.
help.exam: Asking politely for something and answering the price question is part of A1 exam speaking — and of every visit to a bakery.

help.hook: Buy cheese, bread and a bottle of wine at a German market, and understand exactly what the seller says it costs.
help.intro: Shopping needs two small word groups of its own: measures and weights, and money. German measures are simpler than English ones in one way — there is no 'of': ein Kilo Äpfel, eine Flasche Wasser, ein Stück Kuchen, the thing follows the measure directly — and stricter in another: the measures are nouns with a gender (das Kilo, der Liter, die Flasche, das Stück, die Packung, die Dose, das Glas, die Tasse, das Pfund = 500 g). Prices are euros then cents with no word for the comma: zwei Euro fünfzig; Euro never takes an s. Learn the shop's questions and answers as a script and you can buy anything.

tips.title: Measure + thing, no 'of'
tips.text: ein Kilo Kartoffeln, zwei Liter Milch, eine Flasche Wein, ein Stück Käse, eine Packung Nudeln. Masculine and neuter measures stay singular after a number: zwei Kilo, drei Stück, but feminine ones take a plural: zwei Flaschen, drei Tassen.

examples.de: Ich hätte gern ein Kilo Äpfel und zwei Flaschen Wasser.
examples.en: I'd like a kilo of apples and two bottles of water.

examples.de: Ein Stück Kuchen, bitte.
examples.en: A piece of cake, please.

tips.trap: 'ein Kilo von Äpfeln' is understood but wrong; German simply puts the two nouns side by side.

check.q: Ich hätte gern zwei ____ Saft. (die Flasche)
check.why: Flasche is feminine, so it takes a plural after a number — and German needs no 'of' before the thing.

tips.title: Weights and volumes
tips.text: das Gramm (g), das Pfund (500 g — not the English pound!), das Kilo (kg), der Liter (l). Halves: ein halbes Kilo, ein halber Liter.

examples.de: 500 Gramm Käse, bitte. – Ein Pfund? – Ja, genau.
examples.en: 500 grams of cheese, please. – Half a kilo? – Yes, exactly.

examples.de: Ich brauche einen Liter Milch.
examples.en: I need a litre of milk.

check.q: Ich brauche ein ____ Butter. (500 g)
check.why: A German Pfund is exactly 500 grams — half a kilo, not the English pound.

tips.title: Prices
tips.text: 2,50 € = zwei Euro fünfzig. 1,99 € = ein Euro neunundneunzig. 3 € = drei Euro. The question: Was kostet das? / Wie viel kostet …? The answer: Das macht / Das kostet …

examples.de: Was kosten die Tomaten? – Ein Pfund kostet zwei Euro zwanzig.
examples.en: What do the tomatoes cost? – A pound costs 2.20 €.

examples.de: Das macht zwei Euro fünfzig.
examples.en: That's 2.50 €.

check.q: The price tag says 3,40 €. Das kostet ____.
check.why: Say the euros, then the cents, with no word for the comma — and Euro never takes an s.

tips.title: The shop script
tips.text: Was darf es sein? → Ich hätte gern … → Sonst noch etwas? → Nein, danke, das ist alles. → Das macht … → Hier bitte. → Danke, auf Wiedersehen.

examples.de: Sonst noch etwas? – Nein, danke. Was macht das? – Vier Euro achtzig.
examples.en: Anything else? – No thanks. How much is that? – 4.80 €.

examples.de: Was darf es sein? – Ich hätte gern ein Kilo Äpfel.
examples.en: What can I get you? – I'd like a kilo of apples.

check.q: The seller asks: Sonst noch etwas? You don't need anything else. What do you say?
check.why: Das ist alles closes your order; Das macht … is what the seller says, not you.

remember: No 'of': ein Kilo Äpfel, eine Tasse Kaffee.
Euro has no plural s; the cents follow with no comma word.

context.de: Auf dem Markt: Guten Tag, ich hätte gern ein Kilo Kartoffeln, ein Pfund Tomaten und 200 Gramm Käse. – Gern. Sonst noch etwas? – Ja, eine Flasche Apfelsaft und zehn Eier. Was macht das? – Das macht acht Euro sechzig. – Hier sind zehn Euro. – Und ein Euro vierzig zurück. Danke!
context.en: At the market: Hello, I'd like a kilo of potatoes, a pound of tomatoes and 200 grams of cheese. – Certainly. Anything else? – Yes, a bottle of apple juice and ten eggs. How much is that? – That's 8.60 €. – Here's ten euros. – And 1.40 € change. Thanks!

mistakes.why: No 'of' between measure and thing.
Euro has no plural form.
Feminine measures take a plural after a number.

help.hook: When you're ill, say what hurts and how you feel — Mein Kopf tut weh is the sentence that gets you help.
help.intro: When you are ill, you need two things first: naming what hurts, and saying how you feel. The pattern for pain is Mein Kopf tut weh — literally 'my head does pain' — with tun (to do) and the body part as subject; plural parts take tun weh: Meine Füße tun weh. Or use Schmerzen: Ich habe Kopfschmerzen, Bauchschmerzen, Zahnschmerzen — the body part glued to Schmerzen. For how you feel: Wie geht es dir? – Mir geht es gut / schlecht / nicht so gut; Ich bin krank / müde; Ich habe Fieber. The doctor's opening line, Was fehlt Ihnen? (what's wrong?), completes the set — a fuller quiz later in the course builds the doctor's visit on this. The first items ask for the body part; the rest ask for what goes round it — mein or meine, tut or tun, and the …schmerzen compound.

tips.title: … tut weh / … tun weh
tips.text: Singular: Mein Kopf tut weh. Der Zahn tut weh. Plural: Meine Beine tun weh. The body part is the subject, so it takes the nominative: mein Arm, meine Hand, mein Knie.

examples.de: Mein Rücken tut weh.
examples.en: My back hurts.

examples.de: Meine Ohren tun weh.
examples.en: My ears hurt.

check.q: Meine Augen ____ weh.
check.why: Augen is plural, so the verb is tun: Meine Augen tun weh. One thing hurting would be tut.

tips.title: Ich habe …schmerzen
tips.text: Kopfschmerzen, Bauchschmerzen, Halsschmerzen, Zahnschmerzen, Rückenschmerzen — a compound with Schmerzen, always plural, with haben.

examples.de: Ich habe Kopfschmerzen und Fieber.
examples.en: I have a headache and a temperature.

examples.de: Mein Kind hat Bauchschmerzen.
examples.en: My child has a stomach ache.

check.q: Your throat hurts: Ich habe ____.
check.why: Body part + Schmerzen makes one word, always plural, with haben: Ich habe Halsschmerzen.

tips.title: How you feel
tips.text: Wie geht es dir / Ihnen? – Gut / Nicht so gut / Schlecht. Ich bin krank / müde / erkältet. Ich habe Fieber / Husten / Schnupfen. Gute Besserung! = get well soon.

examples.de: Wie geht es dir? – Nicht so gut, ich bin erkältet.
examples.en: How are you? – Not so good, I've got a cold.

examples.de: Wie geht es Ihnen? – Danke, gut.
examples.en: How are you? – Fine, thanks.

check.q: Wie geht es dir? You have a cold. Which answer fits?
options: Nicht so gut, ich bin erkältet.
Nicht so gut, ich habe erkältet.
Nicht so gut, mir bin erkältet.
check.answer: Nicht so gut, ich bin erkältet.
check.why: erkältet goes with sein: ich bin erkältet, just like ich bin krank or ich bin müde.

tips.title: The genders of the body
tips.text: der Kopf, der Arm, der Bauch, der Rücken, der Zahn, der Fuß, der Hals; die Hand, die Nase; das Bein, das Auge, das Ohr, das Knie. Mein or meine follows the gender: mein Kopf, meine Hand, mein Bein.

examples.de: Meine Hand und mein Fuß tun weh.
examples.en: My hand and my foot hurt.

examples.de: Mein Kopf tut weh, und meine Nase auch.
examples.en: My head hurts, and my nose too.

tips.trap: the same body part has a different gender in German than your instinct says. 'die Kopf' is the classic slip.

check.q: ____ Bein tut weh.
check.why: It's das Bein, a neuter noun, so the subject form is mein: Mein Bein tut weh.

remember: One thing hurts: tut weh. Two or more: tun weh.
Kopf + Schmerzen = Kopfschmerzen — body part in front, always plural.

context.de: Guten Tag, Frau Berg, was fehlt Ihnen? – Mein Hals tut weh und ich habe Kopfschmerzen. Ich bin sehr müde. – Haben Sie Fieber? – Ja, 38,5. – Dann bleiben Sie zwei Tage zu Hause und trinken Sie viel Tee. Gute Besserung! – Danke, Herr Doktor.
context.en: Hello, Mrs Berg, what's the matter? – My throat hurts and I have a headache. I'm very tired. – Do you have a temperature? – Yes, 38.5. – Then stay home for two days and drink lots of tea. Get well soon! – Thank you, doctor.

mistakes.why: Pain is expressed with tun, not sein.
Plural subject → tun.
The …schmerzen compounds are always plural.

help.hook: Read a short travel story and find the four facts every trip needs: when, how long, how much and how.
help.intro: A family takes a trip to Munich: train, departure time, ticket price, journey length, hotel, sights, weather. This text carries the core words of travel — der Zug, der Bahnhof, die Fahrkarte, das Hotel, abfahren, dauern, kosten — together with the two things you always need to know about a journey: when and how much. Read once for the story, then answer question by question; look for the time after um, the price before Euro, the length after dauert, and the transport after mit dem.

tips.title: Four questions, four signals
tips.text: Wann? → um neun Uhr. Wie viel? → vierzig Euro. Wie lange? → dauert vier Stunden. Womit? → mit dem Zug.

examples.de: Der Zug fährt um neun Uhr am Bahnhof ab.
examples.en: The train leaves the station at nine.

examples.de: Die Reise dauert vier Stunden.
examples.en: The journey takes four hours.

check.q: 'Der Bus fährt um zehn Uhr ab. Die Fahrt dauert zwei Stunden.' Wie lange dauert die Fahrt?
check.why: Wie lange? is answered after dauert; um zehn Uhr answers Wann?

tips.title: mit dem … — how you travel
tips.text: mit dem Zug, mit dem Bus, mit dem Auto, mit dem Fahrrad — but zu Fuß (on foot). The dative dem is a chunk to recognise, not yet to build.

examples.de: Sie fahren mit dem Zug.
examples.en: They travel by train.

examples.de: Der Zug fährt um neun Uhr am Bahnhof ab.
examples.en: The train leaves the station at nine.

check.q: Anna fährt ____ Fahrrad zur Arbeit. (by bike)
check.why: How you travel is mit dem + vehicle: mit dem Fahrrad. Only on foot is zu Fuß.

tips.title: Where they stay: wohnen in + hotel
tips.text: In München wohnen sie in einem Hotel im Zentrum. wohnen is used for a stay as well as for living somewhere.

examples.de: In München wohnen sie in einem Hotel im Zentrum.
examples.en: In Munich they stay in a hotel in the centre.

examples.de: Am Abend essen sie in einem Restaurant.
examples.en: In the evening they eat at a restaurant.

check.q: 'Wir wohnen drei Tage in einem Hotel in Hamburg.' What does wohnen mean here?
check.why: wohnen is used for a short stay too: three days in a hotel is a stay, not a home.

remember: um = when, Euro = how much, dauert = how long, mit dem = how.
nach + city for 'to a city': nach München, nach Berlin.
help.exam: Timetables, prices and short travel stories are typical A1 exam reading texts — and what you read when you book a trip.

help.hook: Flat ads, bike ads, course notices: learn to spot the one number or word you need without reading every line.
help.intro: Three small ads — a flat, a bicycle, a course — of the kind that fill notice boards and websites, written in the telegram style ads use: no full sentences, just nouns, numbers and abbreviations. Reading them is scanning, not reading: the question names a thing (Preis, Tag, Zimmer) and you find the number next to that word. The abbreviations are the whole point — m² (Quadratmeter), Tel., ab (from), bis (until), pro Monat (per month), zu vermieten / zu verkaufen (to rent / for sale), Anmeldung (registration). Read the questions first, then hunt.

tips.title: Ads have no sentences — scan for the noun
tips.text: Preis → look for Euro. Wann → look for a day or a time. Wie viele → look for a number before a plural noun (2 Zimmer). The answer is always next to its key word.

examples.de: 2 Zimmer, Küche, Bad, 60 m²
examples.en: 2 rooms, kitchen, bathroom, 60 m²

examples.de: Montag und Mittwoch, 18–20 Uhr
examples.en: Monday and Wednesday, 6–8 pm

check.q: „Sprachkurs: Dienstag, 19–21 Uhr, 8 Wochen“ — When are the lessons?
check.why: A 'when' question wants a day and a time: Dienstag, 19–21 Uhr. The 8 belongs to Wochen — how long, not when.

tips.title: The ad vocabulary
tips.text: zu vermieten (to rent), zu verkaufen (for sale), ab (from a date), bis (until), pro Monat (per month), nur (only), fast neu (almost new), Besichtigung (viewing), Anmeldung (registration), Kosten (cost).

examples.de: Ab 1. März. Anmeldung bis 1. April.
examples.en: From 1 March. Registration by 1 April.

examples.de: Fahrrad zu verkaufen: rot, fast neu, nur 80 Euro.
examples.en: Bicycle for sale: red, almost new, only 80 euros.

check.q: „Wohnung zu vermieten“ — What does the ad offer?
check.why: zu vermieten means 'to rent out'; for sale would be zu verkaufen.

tips.title: Several numbers, one right one
tips.text: The flat ad has 2, 60, 650, 1 and a phone number. The question tells you which one you want: pro Monat → 650. Don't grab the first number you see.

examples.de: 650 Euro pro Monat — not 60 (m²), not 2 (Zimmer)
examples.en: 650 euros per month

examples.de: Kosten: 120 Euro. Anmeldung bis 1. April.
examples.en: Cost: 120 euros. Registration by 1 April — two numbers, two questions.

check.q: „Zimmer, 18 m², 3. Stock, 390 Euro pro Monat“ — How much is the rent?
check.why: Rent is a monthly price, so look for the number next to Euro pro Monat. 18 is the size, 3 the floor.

remember: Question first, then hunt the key word; the number beside it is the answer.
'nur am Wochenende' — nur (only) restricts the answer; it is usually the tested word.
help.exam: Short ads and signs are a typical A1 exam reading text — and what you scan on every notice board and flat website.

help.hook: Chat about your everyday life, your routine, your shopping, what you must and want to do, in full German sentences.
help.intro: The closing conversation of this module, in your own AI assistant with voice on: your everyday life — your routine and times, what you buy, what you can and must do. Copy the exercise in, say 'Los geht's', and answer in full sentences; the corrections and the score come at the end. This conversation pulls together the core of the module. The tutor listens for the accusative after haben/kaufen/brauchen, the possessives, the infinitive at the end after a modal, the separable prefix at the end, and times with um / am / halb.

tips.title: Build the sentence around the bracket
tips.text: Modal at 2, infinitive at the end: Ich muss um acht Uhr arbeiten. Separable verb: Ich stehe um sieben auf. Say the last word firmly — it is the part the tutor scores.

examples.de: Am Samstag will ich lange schlafen und dann einkaufen.
examples.en: On Saturday I want to sleep in and then go shopping.

examples.de: Ich muss um acht Uhr arbeiten.
examples.en: I have to work at eight.

check.q: Which sentence is correct? (I have to work early tomorrow.)
check.why: The modal muss sits in position 2 and the infinitive arbeiten goes to the very end.

tips.title: Times and days with their prepositions
tips.text: um halb acht, am Montag, im Sommer. Say the preposition every time; leaving it out is the most common speaking error at this level.

examples.de: Ich frühstücke um halb acht und am Wochenende um zehn.
examples.en: I have breakfast at 7:30 and at the weekend at ten.

examples.de: Im Sommer fahre ich am Wochenende oft weg.
examples.en: In summer I often go away at the weekend.

check.q: I go to the office at half past eight: Ich gehe ____ halb neun ins Büro.
check.why: Clock times take um, and halb neun is a clock time (8:30).

tips.title: Keep going
tips.text: If you don't know a word, describe it or say 'Wie sagt man …?' and move on. Fluency counts; silence doesn't.

examples.de: Ich kaufe … äh … Brot, Milch und Obst.
examples.en: I buy … er … bread, milk and fruit.

examples.de: Wie sagt man … ? Ah, ja: die Waschmaschine!
examples.en: How do you say …? Ah yes: the washing machine!

check.q: You want to say 'fridge' (Kühlschrank) but the word won't come. What is the best thing to say?
options: Wie sagt man …? Das Ding für kalte Milch!
check.answer: Wie sagt man …? Das Ding für kalte Milch!
check.why: Describing the word in simple German keeps the conversation going, and fluency counts more than one missing word.

remember: Whole sentences, verb at the end where it belongs.
Ask back — 'Und du?' — it is scored as interaction.
help.exam: Talking about your routine, shopping and plans is the heart of A1 exam speaking — and of small talk with neighbours.

help.hook: Say where you're heading, to Berlin, to the cinema, to the doctor, to grandma's, and pick nach, in or zu.
help.intro: Wo? asks where something is; Wohin? asks where it is going — and German answers the second question with three different prepositions. nach is for towns and for countries without an article (nach Berlin, nach Spanien) and for home (nach Hause). in is for countries that have an article (in die Schweiz, in die USA) and for places you go into: ins Kino, in die Stadt, in den Park, in die Schule. zu is for people (zu Anna, zu meiner Oma) and for places you go to rather than into — zum Arzt, zur Arbeit, zum Bahnhof. After in the article is accusative (in den Park), after zu it is dative (zum = zu dem, zur = zu der); for now you learn these as chunks. The contrast with Wo? is the heart of it: ich bin zu Hause, but ich gehe nach Hause; ich bin im Kino, but ich gehe ins Kino.

tips.title: nach — cities, countries without article, home
tips.text: nach Berlin, nach Wien, nach Spanien, nach Deutschland — and nach Hause. No article ever follows nach here.

examples.de: Wir fahren morgen nach Berlin.
examples.en: We're going to Berlin tomorrow.

examples.de: Es ist spät. Ich gehe jetzt nach Hause.
examples.en: It's late. I'm going home now.

tips.trap: English 'to' covers all three. 'Ich gehe zu Berlin' or 'nach Kino' are the classic errors.

check.q: Tomorrow I'm going to Vienna: Morgen fahre ich ____ Wien.
check.why: Towns and cities take nach, with no article after it.

tips.title: in + article — into a place, and countries with an article
tips.text: ins Kino (in das), in die Stadt, in den Park, in die Schule — and in die Schweiz, in die Türkei, in die USA. The masculine article becomes den.

examples.de: Heute Abend gehen wir ins Kino.
examples.en: Tonight we're going to the cinema.

examples.de: Am Sonntag gehen wir in den Park.
examples.en: On Sunday we're going to the park.

check.q: Today I'm going into town: Ich gehe heute ____ Stadt.
check.why: A place you go into takes in plus the article; Stadt is feminine, so in die Stadt.

tips.title: zu — people and destinations
tips.text: zu Anna, zu meiner Oma; zum Arzt, zum Bahnhof (zu dem), zur Arbeit, zur Schule (zu der). zu is also what you use when you do not go inside: zum Bahnhof, zur Post.

examples.de: Ich bin krank. Ich muss zum Arzt.
examples.en: I'm ill. I have to go to the doctor's.

examples.de: Am Samstag fahre ich zu meiner Oma.
examples.en: On Saturday I'm going to my grandma's.

check.q: Tonight I'm going to Paul's: Ich gehe heute Abend ____ Paul.
check.why: Going to a person always takes zu: zu Paul.

tips.title: nach Hause vs zu Hause
tips.text: nach Hause answers Wohin? (going home); zu Hause answers Wo? (being at home). The same pairs: im Kino / ins Kino, in der Stadt / in die Stadt.

examples.de: Ich gehe nach Hause. – Ich bin zu Hause.
examples.en: I'm going home. – I'm at home.

examples.de: Ich gehe ins Kino. – Ich bin im Kino.
examples.en: I'm going to the cinema. – I'm at the cinema.

check.q: Wo bist du? – Ich bin ____.
check.why: Wo? asks where you are, so the answer is zu Hause; nach Hause is only for going home.

remember: nach for towns, countries and home · in for into (ins Kino, in den Park) · zu for people and places you go to (zum Arzt).
Going home = nach Hause; being at home = zu Hause.

context.de: Was machst du heute? – Am Morgen muss ich zum Arzt. Dann gehe ich in die Stadt und kaufe ein. Am Nachmittag fahre ich zu meiner Oma, und am Abend gehen wir ins Kino. Und im Sommer? – Im Sommer fliegen wir nach Spanien!
context.en: What are you doing today? – In the morning I have to go to the doctor's. Then I'm going into town to do some shopping. In the afternoon I'm going to my grandma's, and in the evening we're going to the cinema. And in the summer? – In the summer we're flying to Spain!

mistakes.why: nach is only for towns, countries without an article and home; a building you go into takes in.
Towns and cities take nach.
zu Hause is where you are; nach Hause is where you are going.

help.hook: Our house, your flat, their dog: with unser, euer and ihr you can talk about things that belong to more than one person.
help.intro: The possessives for more than one owner, and the formal one: unser (our), euer (your — several friends), ihr (their) and Ihr with a capital (your — formal, one person or several). They work exactly like mein: they take the ein-endings, decided by the noun that follows — unser Sohn, unsere Tochter, unsere Kinder, and in the accusative unseren Sohn. Two details make them tricky. euer loses its second e as soon as an ending is added: euer Hund, but eure Katze, euren Hund. And ihr / Ihr is the same word in speech: in writing the capital decides between 'their' and 'your (formal)', and in speech the situation does — Herr Braun, ist das Ihr Koffer? The quiz gives you the owner in brackets; choose the word and add the ending for the noun.

tips.title: Owner first
tips.text: wir → unser · ihr (you all) → euer · sie (they) → ihr · Sie → Ihr. Then the ending comes from the noun, as with mein.

examples.de: Das ist unser Haus.
examples.en: That is our house.

examples.de: Tom und Lisa verkaufen ihre Wohnung.
examples.en: Tom and Lisa are selling their flat.

check.q: Wir haben ein Auto. Das ist ____ Auto.
check.why: The owner is wir, so the possessive is unser. euer belongs to ihr (you all), ihr to sie (they).

tips.title: The endings: nothing, -e, -en
tips.text: der/das-noun (nominative): no ending — unser Sohn, euer Auto. die-noun and plural: -e — unsere Tochter, eure Kinder. der-noun as an object: -en — unseren Garten, euren Schlüssel.

examples.de: Unsere Kinder spielen im Garten.
examples.en: Our children are playing in the garden.

examples.de: Wir lieben unseren Garten.
examples.en: We love our garden.

check.q: Wir besuchen ____ Großvater. (der Großvater)
check.why: Großvater is masculine and the object of besuchen, so the ending is -en: unseren.

tips.title: euer drops an e
tips.text: euer + ending = eur-: eure Lehrerin, euren Hund. unser keeps both e’s: unsere, unseren.

examples.de: Kinder, wo ist eure Lehrerin?
examples.en: Children, where's your teacher?

examples.de: Habt ihr euren Schlüssel?
examples.en: Do you have your key?

tips.trap: 'euere' and 'euern' look logical but are not the standard forms; write eure, euren.

check.q: Kinder, wo sind ____ Bücher?
check.why: Plural nouns take -e, and euer drops its second e when an ending is added: eure.

tips.title: Ihr with a capital = your (formal)
tips.text: Talking to someone you call Sie, the possessive is Ihr / Ihre / Ihren — capital I, like Sie.

examples.de: Herr Braun, ist das Ihr Koffer?
examples.en: Mr Braun, is that your suitcase?

examples.de: Frau Weber, wie ist Ihre Telefonnummer?
examples.en: Mrs Weber, what's your phone number?

check.q: Herr Lang, wo wohnen ____ Eltern? (you say Sie to him)
check.why: For someone you call Sie, 'your' is Ihr with a capital; Eltern is plural, so it takes -e: Ihre.

remember: unser – euer – ihr – Ihr: our, your (all), their, your (formal).
euer + ending loses an e: eure, euren.

context.de: Das ist unser Haus, und das ist unser Garten. Unsere Kinder spielen oft hier. Und ihr? Wie ist eure Wohnung? Habt ihr euren Balkon schon fertig? – Ja! Und Frau Klein, ist das Ihr Hund? – Nein, das ist der Hund von Tom und Lisa. Ihr Hund heißt Bello.
context.en: This is our house, and this is our garden. Our children often play here. And you? What's your flat like? Have you finished your balcony yet? – Yes! And Mrs Klein, is that your dog? – No, that's Tom and Lisa's dog. Their dog is called Bello.

mistakes.why: Tochter is a die-noun, so the possessive takes -e.
Opa is a der-noun and the object: -en.

mistakes.wrong: Herr Braun, ist das ihr Koffer?
mistakes.right: Herr Braun, ist das Ihr Koffer?
mistakes.why: Formal your is written with a capital I.

help.hook: Tickets, times, prices and the post office: learn these everyday words with their der, die or das and errands get easier.
help.intro: Every word this module's exercises use, on one deck of flashcards: 166 cards, 69 of them nouns. The vocabulary of this module is everyday nouns, the core verbs and the small words that hold a sentence together, from the themes Tagesablauf, Uhrzeit, Kalender, Reisen & Verkehr: tickets, Durchsagen, Einkaufen: Mengen, Maße, Währung, Dienstleistungen: Post, Bank. Write the German, choose it from four options, or flip the card and rate yourself. A word you miss comes back later in the same run, and stays in your weak words until you get it right three times in a row.

tips.title: Say the article as part of the word
tips.text: At this level almost every noun is new, and its gender is a fact to memorise. Say der, die or das aloud with the noun every time, so the two stay welded together.

examples.de: der Mann, Plural: ¨-er
examples.en: man

examples.de: der Tisch, Plural: -e
examples.en: table

check.q: You are learning the word for 'key'. What should you say aloud?
check.why: The gender can't be guessed reliably, so say the article with the noun every time until they stick together.

tips.title: Three modes, three kinds of memory
tips.text: Choose trains recognition, Write trains recall, and Flip trains honesty with yourself. Start a new deck in Choose, move to Write once most cards feel familiar, and use Flip for a fast review before a lesson or a trip.

examples.de: der Hund, Plural: -e
examples.en: dog

examples.de: der Apfel, Plural: ¨-
examples.en: apple

check.q: die Fahrkarte means …?
check.why: Recalling a meaning on your own builds stronger memory than spotting it. die Fahrkarte is the ticket; der Fahrplan is the timetable.

tips.title: A noun without its article is marked wrong
tips.text: In Write mode a noun only counts with der, die or das in front of it. The card tells you when you had the right word but left the article off, so you know exactly what to fix.

examples.de: der Ball, Plural: ¨-e
examples.en: ball

examples.de: die Frau, Plural: -en
examples.en: woman

check.q: At the post office you need a stamp. Which is the complete word?
check.why: A noun is only complete with its article. Briefmarke is feminine: die Briefmarke.

remember: Never say a noun without its article, not even in your head.
Miss a word? It comes back in the same run. Three correct answers in a row take it off the weak list.
Verbs and adjectives have no article: type them as they stand, like "mich".
